Before the notices of motion are called, I would like to mention that at some early date I propose to inquire as to what is the rule in the several departments respecting the holding of municipal offices by government employees, and I give notice now so that the government may be prepared to give information. My object is to ascertain what is the practice in each department, and the reason I bring this up is that in my own constituency, a man, who has a salary of $150 as preventive officer, out of which he has to provide his own office, fuel and lighting, and whose official duties take up very little of his time, was elected to the municipal council of the county of Halifax, and was obliged, under an order in council, to resign either that office or his office in the Customs Department. He knew nothing about any such practice previously, but some one made a report to the department, and the department called on him to resign either his office in the customs, or his position as municipal councillor. I am not criticising, but I am simply suggesting that there ought to be some uniform practice followed, because in the city of Ottawa I understand that there are three members of the city council who are employees of this government drawing salaries which recompense them for the whole of their time. There ought to be a distinct, uniform practice applicable to all the departments, although I recognize that perhaps in some respects one department may afford ground for some distinction on special considerations not applicable to others.

THE PORTSMOUTH PENITENTIARY. Mr. EDWARDS. I would like to call attention to an editorial in the Kingston " Standard.'
The hon. gentleman [DOT]cannot on notice of motion without the consent of the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Go on.

I must thank the House for giving me this privilege. I think the matter I am about to bring up is one of importance, not only to the people of Ontario, but to the people of every province, inasmuch as it affects the good name of this *country on the other side of the line. The article referred to calls attention to the fact that a prisoner liberated from the Portsmouth penitentiary and deported by order of this government to the United States, was taken to Ogdensburg by the government agent, taken across the line there and given his liberty without a cent of money in his pocket and without any overcoat or warm clothing of any kind. I have taken the trouble to make some inquiries, and I find this is not an isolated ease. A few days later, when the thermometer registered 10 below zero, another prisoner was liberated and sent out of jail without even an overcoat. When a man has finished his sentence and is liberated, we take it for granted that he intends to lead a better life, but to send him out in that manner is making it almost impossible for him to do better. The immigration agent advised this man, when he got to Ogdensburg, to go to the mayor, tell him he was an exconvict just liberated from Portsmouth penitentiary, and that he had no money and insufficient clothing for that kind of weather, and to ask for lodging and food. To set a man at liberty at this season of the year, and then advise him to go and brand himself as an ex-convict does seem to me to be inhuman in every sense. This is a matter, I am sure, that the government would not wish to see repeated, and I call attention to it in the hope that nothing of the kind will occur again.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The circumstance to which the hon. member (Mr. Edwards) has referred, was brought to my attention by receiving through the post a copy of a newspaper in which the facts were stated and editorial opinion expressed. At once the warden of the penitentiary was communicated with and asked for a statement as to the facts of the case. The first mention of the matter in the newspaper took place, I think, on Saturday of last week, though it was referred to again on Monday of this week, and the first knowledge of the circumstances in Ottawa was. on Monday or Tuesday of this week. So, the report of the warden of the penitentiary has not yet reached me. I, therefore, am not able to say anything with authority in regard to the circumstances. I should like, however, to point out to the House that, so far as the deporting of this man, or any man, from Canada, is concerned, the administration of our statute in that regard is, of course, in the hands of the immigration authorities. The circumstance that any one coming into this country from another country has, within a limited time after reaching this country, become an inmate of a prison is, in itself, ground for ordering his deportation as soon as his sentence of imprisonment may have expired. And, so far as the deportation to his home country of such a man is concerned, the penitentiaries administration has nothing to do with it. The prisoner serves his time, and when his sentence has expired he is released, and, if he is at that time liable to be deported by reason of having offended against the laws of Canada, the immigration department, by its officials, takes charge of the man and sees to his deportation, exactly as would have been done at an earlier stage if he had never been in prison at all. So that, so far as the deportation of this particular man is concerned, the authorities of the penitentiaries, as distinguished from the authorities of the Immigration Department, are not responsible.
And, in regard to the circumstances under which any prisoner in the penitentiary whose sentence has expired is liberated, our Penitentiaries Act governs, and I have no idea that in this case it will be found that there has been any transgression by the warden or other officials of the penitentiary of the provisions of our general law. It may be that our Penitentiaries Act, in speaking generally of the amount of money and the amount of clothing which shall be given to any prisoner upon his discharge has not taken into consideration the differences in temperature between discharge in midwinter and discharge in midsummer. It may be that special provision ought rto be made for the issuing of a larger amount of clothing to a prisoner whose sentence expires in midwinter; but it is, of course, apparent that it is im-

possible to regulate beforehand what the necessities of any particular case may be, because it is within the knowledge of all of us that there may happen, and often does happen to be, even in the month of January and in the depth of our winter, a day, a week, or even a longer period, during whiph the absence 'of the heavier clothing would not be felt by the discharged convict.

speakeroldname: Mr. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Portage la Prairie) moved:
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this House, a substantial reduction in the import duties on agricultural implements is now due the agriculturists of Canada, and is in just accord with the true ends of a protective tariff.
He said: The subject launched in the resolution which I now have the honour to move, occupies a position of supreme importance in the commercial life of this country. For close upon a third of a century, the basic principle which should govern our fiscal system and the application of that principle to the details of our importations has been canvassed more thoroughly than has any other subject in the political history of Canada. Throughout that time, the party with which I am now associated has planted its faith on those foundations of economic belief laid down by the founder of the party himself and now recognized as the fiscal system known as the national policy. To that fiscal system, the party to which I have the honour to belong has, in my humble belief, consistently throughout all these years adhered; and to that fiscal system, fully stated-to the national policy, I say, fully stated, stated in the language of Sir John Macdonald himself and repeated in the words of his successors, and illustrated by the practices of his successors, to that policy, stated wholly and not partially-I am still proud to adhere. What has been the course of the party now in office, and what has been their fiscal theory, I shall not trust myself at present to discuss. But you will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, from the occurrences, particularly of the last feVv months, that no argument will appeal at this time, to either side of the House that has not its footing in a sane and reasonable protective policy. I say that because, in my humble belief, there is no member on either side of the House to-day who would not be compelled to acknowledge, to himself at least, that, under the conditions that now obtain on this continent, a sane and reasonable protective policy is the

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
only one possible for Canada. Perhaps in that statement I could have excepted the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), who is yet an exotic in this country, and who, I sincerely believe,, still manages by assiduous care to keep alive his free trade theories. But with that exception, I am safe, I believe, in saying that the mask is . now pretty largely thrown off, and that every member of this House, even on the other side, actually does acknowledge in his inmost heart that nothing but a sane and reasonable protection is possible under present continental conditions.
Now, Sir, it may be possible, and I believe it is a fact, that there are some hon. gentlemen opposite who have no fiscal belief of any kind, and I am not surprised that men who have followed that party have been confused by its tortuous course throughout these years, and in despair at the double life it was leading, consorting with protection while under marital vows to free trade, have become economic athiests. For my part I believe there is only one footing on which an argument can possibly be based in regard to any change of our present fiscal system. This has been impressed upon me toy occurrences during the last few months. A short time ago we had one thousand or more of the agriculturists of Canada waiting upon this government, and at considerable length assailing the First Minister and his cabinet for continuing, as they believed, in a more pronounced form than had ever been done before, the principle of protection in our fiscal system. Without a dissenting voice they asserted as an assumption that could not be denied that the protective system, whether it were good or bad, was more pronounced in the present tariff than it was in that of the Conservative government. On the other hand, what do we find later? A delegation representing the manufacturers of Canada came to Ottawa, and in a well matured presentation of their case they assumed, as. a basis, that the same fiscal system which now prevails had obtained for thirty years in Canada. To neither one argument or the other did the Prime Minister, who replied, offer any word of resentment or dispute. He did not dare to tell those thousand agriculturists that he had eliminated the protective principle from our tariff; nor did he dare to say to those thousand men that he had moved one hair's breadth towards eliminating the protective principle from our tariff. Nor did he dare to resent the statement of that body of manufacturers that the very same system prevails now that has prevailed for thirty years. Consequently, I am not out of the way when I assume as a starting point that the only argument that can prevail on either side is an argument based on the

essential necessity of a sane and reasonable protection.
Now, Sir. the charge I have to make against the government in this connection is not the gravest charge that can be laid at their doors. The gravest charge which history will always hold against this government is that they preached a doctrine in which they had no real belief, is that they professed in infidelity hostility to the policy which they knew was the only one practicable for this country, and thereby acquired office by false prentises and deceit, and that for fourteen years they have worn the mask of hypocrisy, ever getting thinner and thinner, until now it has literally blown away. But the charge I have to make, and which I hope to bring home to the government this afternoon is not that one, though it is the most serious; it is this, that in their attempts to continue the National Policy which had obtained for years before, they have overlooked, they have neglected one essential feature of that policy, they have quite forgotten its guiding principle, namely, the principle that as our industrial institutions advanced in strength and as they were able with every advance to acquire a hold on the home market, the import duties were to be diminished and adjusted in order to meet the evolving and changing conditions. It is that restraining, guiding principle which I claim this government has entirely overlooked, and as a consequence they have allowed, in the respect which I am discussing this afternoon, protection to run rampant, and they have for reasons that are only too obvious, become the slaves of those who helped them into power and who now maintain them there behind ramparts of gold.
Now, I referred a few moments ago to what was the outstanding principle which I maintain this government has failed to implement, and I will lay that on the records in a very simple, and I think thorough way. I would quote briefly from the language of that distinguished statesman whose title to greatness in this country is becoming clearer and stronger as the fruits of his labours multiply; I will quote the words of Sir John A. Macdonald, found in a speech made in this House in 1878, at page 857 of the ' Hansard.' Speaking on the 8th of March, Sir John A. Macdonald uttered these words:
If we had a protective system in this country, if we had a developed capital, we could, by giving our manufacturers a reasonable hold on our home trade, attain a higher position among the nations.
Further on:-
I do not mean that we should adopt a tariff like that of the United States, hut one such as the necessities of Canada demand.
And still further on:-
It can wTell be understood that a judicious tariff may, on the whole, he a moderate tariff.
So that the basic principle was laid down in so far as the feature I am now emphasizing goes, was that the object of that tariff was to give the manufacturing industries of Canada a reasonable hold on the home market. The same principle was supported by Sir Leonard Tilley at page 429 of * Hansard,' 1879, when, on the 14th March, he made his budget speech introducing the National Policy. With a consistency of which w7e are proud the Finance Ministers who succeeded in office carried out the same doctrine there laid down. I quote now from the words of the present hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), who at the time they were uttered was Finance Minister of Canada. I quote these words from the ' Hansard,' of that time. I do not do so with any particular personal object, I do not know as to how iar he may agree with me as to the application of the principle which be there repeated, but I do know that the principle which he there laid down he is the man not to fall away from now. At page 194 of ' Hansard ' of 1894 Mr. Foster made the following remarks:
If there is to he a protective system at all. everybody knows that it must he higher in its inception than as the years gradually pass, when industries have become established and when the industrial development of the country grows apace.
Further, at page 202:
I wish to state as forcibly as possible that the argument is completely baseless, that the policy of protection depends on the percentage of impost that shall be put on a certain article because the government recognizes as all people recognize, that the conditions of business have changed in the last fourteen years and that it is well to arrange the tariff to suit those changed conditions, and it therefore does not justify the conclusion that the government has gone back on the principle ot protection or discarded the cardinal principle of the National Policy.
And further on, at page 234:
The reduction in agricultural implements
And this has a very particular bearing on the present discussion.
-from 35 per cent to 20 per cent, is one under which it would tax the ingenuity of the manufacturer to keep the field against what is now keen competition especially in the Northwest.
Thus did he postulate that the test by which these duties were to be judged, the guide by which he was to be governed was such a duty as, at the narrowest point, would test the ingenuity of the manufacturers to keep the field against foreign competition and clearly laying it down that as the conditions of business improve and as

their hold became stronger the same principle would compel a reduction to meet those conditions. And, Sir, at page 202, the following remarks were also made by the same hon. gentleman.
Our industries have not yet overtaken the home consumption of the people, but are gradually growing up to the point of meeting the consumptive demand in the country.
Applying also the clear test as to whether or not these manufacturers had what Sir John A. Macdonald called a reasonable hold on the home market. I refer also, because the words are particularly in point, to the remarks made by the present hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. J. Haggart) who was at that time, I believe, Minister of Railways and Canals in the government of Sir John Thompson. The hon. member for South Lanark, at page 347, made the statement that by reason of the vastly growing exports abroad the manufacturers had demonstrated their ability to stand reductions. Further and more particularly is this the quotation that I wish to call attention to, the hon. gentleman said, as will be found at page 347 of ' Hansard ':
For the last fourteen years, protection in Canada has so developed our manufactures that the government now think that a fair reduction in the tariff be ventured on. They believe that our people can compete with less protection.than formerly, and to prove that, it can be pointed out that we are now sending agricultural implements to many portions of the world.
There the hon. member for South Lanark clearly laid it down that the test to be applied was as to whether or not the purpose of the protective system had been served and that the measure in which it had been served was the relative degree of the export trade to the home consumption, particular reference there being made to the large export trade in agricultural implements. I will ask the House to bear this especially in mind because later on in what I have to say I will be able to convince you simply by the fewest figures that the export trade in agricultural implements at that date when the duty was reduced by 15 per cent was almost as nothing compared with the huge export trade which these manufacturers have been able to work up under the protection afforded them by the apostles of free trade.
I call the attention of the House to the present conditions with regard to agricultural implements. I have chosen this field not because there is nothing else that could be the subject for attack, but because observation has shown me that a very strong argument can be made in that field and because also, it seems to me, a better purpose can be served by a clear cut and definite discussion of one class of business rather than by a rambling one over the whole Mr. MEIGHEN.
field of our tariff list. Now, in the sphere of agricultural implements, I want to make it clear, I include all the larger agricultural implements. I do not include mere tools, spades, forks, and so on, but I take such a class as are generally and commonly understood by those who themselves use them as distinctly appertaining to the farm, being distinctly agricultural implements, and I make this premise before I further proceed that it will become clearer as I go on that what argument I have to make will not apply with equal force even to all of these. additional Chinese wall, if you may call it such that this government has seen fit, in violation of every principle of public honour and of its own, to hedge round the manufacturers of the articles I have mentioned, and which enables them to make a profit after leaping over these tariff walls of considerable height in all these countries.
I have only this finally to say:	I have
appended to my resolution a clause which states that a reduction in these duties now is consistent with the best ends of a protective tariff, and I found my argument on that. I believe it is the principle which really does and which ought to prevail. If any hon. gentleman opposite can base it on another principle let him do so. But, I invite his assistance to the cause. I invite every man in this House, for whatever reasons may be to him compelling, to seek the same goal as I seek. And, Sir, if the discussion this afternoon has to be cut short under the rules of the House, I invite the government to give an opportunity, as they have the power to do, for a further discussion of the matter at an early date in the session. Mr. Speaker, we have listened as I am sure we all expected we would listen, to the hon. gentleman's exposition of his views on this important subject, with the very greatest interest. And, while we may differ from the hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) in this

and many other matters I think every person in this House would agree it is no flattery to the hon. member to say that he carefully and conscientiously prepared the remarks which he desires to offer to the House, and that he presents them, as far as he is able to, in a spirit of fairness. I shall not refer to the very large portion of his address which was taken up in dealing with statistics of the trade and commerce returns; I shall rather endeavour to deal with that principle which seemed to permeate every sentence the hon. gentleman uttered, and which seems to be the guiding principle of his faith, namely, his devotion to the old Tory doctrine of protection. The hon. gentleman has stated that there was in his opinion only one member of this House on either side who was opposed to the principle of protection, and if I understood him aright he desired to place himself on record as believing . that every colleague of his on the Conservative side, and that every member on this side, apart from the hon. member from Bed Deer (Mr. Clark), was a protectionist. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) will forgive me if I ask him, if, he should again talk along that line, he will kindly honour me with a place beside the hon.'member from Bed Deer as being a man who is opposed to protection.
Now, Mr. Speaker, at this juncture, when we have had what we may call a record breaking delegation of my own constituents and of the hon. gentleman's constituents, and of the people of the west generally; when we have had, to a certain extent, the cabinet worked up over our declaration of principles, and, perhaps, coming to our way of thought, and desirous to meet the wishes of our agricultural constituents, I regret that the first voice to be heard in this Chamber advocating and supporting that abominable doctrine of protection should be the voice of a man who is sent here by the agriculturists of the riding of Portage la Prairie. I believe that his constituents and the constituents generally of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta will regard with great surprise and strong protest that he should, in the face of this House, be the first to place himself on record as a devoted and decided protectionist. With regard to that portion of the hon. gentleman's motion -which deals only with a reduction of the duties at the present time, I have no great quarrel. I do not regard it all in the same light as he does, but I think that, perhaps unconsciously, he has juggled the figures. However, he has studied his figures and I have not, and, I will not deal with the great -volume of figures he has presented to the House. But, even to, an amateur as I am in such a matter, it occurs to me as very strange that in the hon. gentleman's comparison with Mr. KNOWLES.
regard to the value of binders and the duty upon binders, taking, as he did, in each case, not the ad valorem, but the dollars and cents duty, he neglected to tell the House that the binder which is used to-day is without the slightest question a great deal more valuable binder than was used in the days when the Conservative party went out of power. Then an eight-foot binder was practically unknown, but to-day an eight-foot binder is in general use, and it is one-third as much again in its operating power, one-third as strong in its build, and one-third more valuable than the binder to which the hon. gentleman had reference as being in use when the Conservatives went out of power in 1896. May I also call the attention of my hon. friend to what I think was a great oversight on his part, and it is that he devoted himself in his speech altogether to the question of agricultural implements. I would like to ask him if there are not many other things as to which the same spirit of justice would require to have the duty lowered. For illustration, he tells us that there are a million odd dollars' worth of agricultural implements imported *to this country annually, and he also tells us that there are $17,000,000, worth of cotton goods imported. Why should not the good wife on the farm receive the same kindly assistance from my hon. friend as her husband does? Why should she not be given the same opportunity to go to the open market and buy as cheaply as she may of the goods which are required for the farmer's household as her husband should have to buy the agricultural implements he needs on the farm? The hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) commenced by placing himself on record as to his views and as to the reasons why he held these views, and I desire, in. as few words as I may, to follow his example in that respect. I am going, if my hon. friend will allow me, to follow his footsteps in that regard, and I shall state what I think of protection. I may say, to commence with, that my thoughts on this subject are not the same as those he entertained. If the hon. gentleman had been a member of this House in 1908, and if he had been in his place here on the first day of June of that year, he would have heard me say the words I am about to read from ' Hansard,' page 9514:-

You did not say that in
speaking to the resolution you had on the Order Paper last session.

Last session did not include the 1st of June, 1908. On that occasion we were dealing with the views which had been presented to this House by the
hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) upon the question of lumber. I then said:

One reason why we are always afraid of the men engaged in lumbering is that there is such danger that they will become com-binesters, and I deliberately state that protection is the mother of trusts and combines. Tariffs breed trusts, and if there is one thing in which there should be no trust, that thing is lumber. For my part, I am against protection from start to finish; protection is to me an abomination. I support the Liberal party because of the two parties it is the one that favours the lower duties. But if a strong party decidedly devoted to free trade were to arise, I would be a supporter of that party regarding its tariff policy. In this House, as representing my constituents, I believe I serve them best by supporting the party that goes the furthest in granting a low tariff.
Those are the words spoken by me, according to my light, on June 1, 1908, and they are the views I still hold and hold more emphatically, notwithstanding the very eloquent defence of protection which we have heard this afternoon.
Allow me also to quote an equally brief extract from my own remarks in the session of 1906-7 at page 1903 of ' Hansard.' We were dealing then with the matter of duty on fruit. My hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) had been advocating the views of the fruit growers of western Ontario. I say there:
It may be that the organization whose views the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) presents, speaks the mind of a large part of the fruitgrowers of Ontario, but in regard to the organizations that throng the corridors here

This was at the time of the revision of the tariff.
-I want to say that I have very little respect for their opinion. I have no doubt that the gentlemen who compose them are as honourable, just and independent as they can be, hut in my opinion the organizations that come here have as aggregations more of the hog spirit in them than they should he found to possess. When they come here and say they cannot earn an honest living without the people paying an artificial price for what they produce, I think we might as well give them a little money, give them what we have to spare as a present and let them go home. I really believe they go too far, and that as individuals they would not ask what they do as organizations. To speak frankly, I do not take any stock in what the Fruit Growers' Associations come down here to ask. As I say, we are willing to pay a reasonable duty to help along our brother farmers, but when my hon. friends opposite ask for an increased duty, I feel that we must oppose it.
Therefore, I, as did my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) place myself on record, not for the first time as he does, but after a course of some years, as being a man against protection and in favour of a party which if possible would give
a tariff which would not protect, but would give us only revenue. Holding that view I have always felt that I could do nothing other than support the Liberal party here, that I could not see my way clear to support the party which for years has_ been advocating and supporting the doctrine of protection. Considerable criticism has been made of the Liberal party on the grouna, as the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) has said, that when they came into power they had pledged themselves to endeavour to obtain a lower tariff, and also to obtain reciprocity with the United States, as though those promises had been entirely unfulfilled. Let me read to the House the planks of the Liberal party when they came into power first on reciprocity and then on the question of lower tariffs generally. The resolution on reciprocity was:
That the Liberal party is prepared to enter into negotiations with a view to obtaining a fair and liberal reciprocity, including a well considered list of manufactured articles.
That was the doctrine and the policy of the Liberal party in the year when they made their appeal to the people of Canada, in 1896, and I submit it is one that the Liberal party is well able to say has been their policy since they came into powei. They have kept an open mind on that subject, they approached the people of the United States and did what they could, in honour and dignity, to obtain better trade relations with the people of the United States.	. .
When our party is criticised it is on the ground that they have failed to carry out to the letter the tariff pledges which they are alleged to have made when they came into power. It is important to know what exactly was their policy to know what were the planks in their pla -form in that year 1893, and I am going to read for the benefit of m-y hon. friends opposite a few words from the plank in that platform of 1893. I read:
That the customs tariff of the Dominion should be based, not as it is now, upon the protective principle, but upon the requirements of the public service; that the highest interests of Canada demand a removal of this obstacle to our country's progress by the adoption of a sound fiscal policy, which, while not doing injustice to any class, will promote domestic find foreign trade, and hasten the return of prosperity to our people.
Here is the part which you might call the affirming part of this same platform.
That to that end the tariff should be reduced to the needs of honest, economical and efficient government. That it should bo so adjusted as to make free, or bear as lightly as possible, upon the necessaries of life, and

should l>e so arranged as to promote freer trade with the whole world, more particularly with Great Britain and the United States.
I wish also to read the words uttered by the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier) then leader of the opposition in dealing with this plank:
X say, the policy should he a policy of free trade such as they have in England, hut I am sorry to say that the circumstances of the country cannot admit at present of that policy in its entirety, hut I propose to you, from this day forward, that it should be the goal to which we aspire. I propose to you from this day, although we cannot adopt the policy itself, to adopt the principle which regulates it; that is to say, that, though it should be your misfortune for many years to come to have to raise a revenue by customs duties, those duties should be levied only so far as is necessary to carry on the business of the government.
I have read these extracts because to my mind they go very far into the root of the matter when we come to deal with as important a question as we are asked to deal with now, when we are told that this government, as the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) says, have been bereft of every sense of honour and have been guilty of every act of infidelity in relation to the trust placed in them by the people of Canada. Hon. gentlemen think, no doubt honestly, that the government had been very derelict in the performance of their duty. Fortunately for 14 years there have been many hundreds of thousands of people in Canada who do not think as the hon. gentlemen think, and I am convinced they will continue to think differently from hon. gentlemen opposite for many years to come. When our party came into power, it was alleged by no less an authority than Sir Charles Tupper and also by his lieutenants that if the Liberal party should be given the reins of office, this country would be brought to the verge of ruin, our factories would have to close, and everything would be dead in the way of business. No doubt Sir Charles Tupper and his party honestly believed in this prophesy. Their policy differed from that which the Liberal party pledged itself to adopt, it differs from that policy yet, and my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) no doubt is opposed to our fiscal policy.
What is the fiscal policy inaugurated by your government?

I do not wish to be discourteous, but I have really something of national importance to deal with, and I would ask my hon. friend not to interrupt. He has often spoken in this House, and 1 have not interrupted him.
Did you say national importance or national policy? "

I desire to place myself on record now, as I have in the past, on this question. I desire to say that although the present government has not gone as far in lowering the tariff as I would like, yet I would give to it what little influence and support I can for I believe that if the party opposite were given power they would plunge heavily into the doctrine of protection.

speechtext: Hear, hear.
How do you know?

I will tell you how. My hon. friend from Portage told us today what he considered was the policy of the Conservative party, and he gave us quotations from what was said by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) some years ago. Of course anything the hon. member for North Toronto says is interesting, but it is news to me that the day has come when that hon. gentleman desires that we should have less protection than formerly. Let me read a comparatively recent statement from him, and which I desire to put on record. Speaking in Hamilton, according to the report in the ' Mail and Empire,' he used these words :
So long as we import into this country $1,500,000 of agricultural implements in less than a year, every one of which might he made by the artisans and labourers of this country, and import that amount from the United States, a market from which our products are shut out by au almost prohibitive tariff; so long as our hinder twine is largely made for us in that country; so long as $11,000,000 manufactured iron and steel are brought in from the United States whilst in Canada the great natural vaults are bursting with iron and coal, and Canadian brawn and intelligence is chafing to unlock them and set these riches and resources loose; so long as our pulp and paper resources are sacrificed in other markets, and we import millions of dollars worth of their manufactured products; so long as the lead smelters of the United States grow rich, whilst they put 1) per cent duty upon lead in ore and 2J per cent upon lead in bullion; so long as these things are unredressed, there is a reason for the existence of the Liberal-Conservative party.
This is the language used by that hon. gentleman to whom my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) turns as his authority for declaring that protection should be now somewhat departed from. Just put the quotations given by my hon. friend side by side with the language I have just read, and I prefer to abide by the later utterance, which I am sure my hon. friend will not question.
I was asked a moment ago what the Conservative party would do if it came into power. All I oan say is that words such as those I have quoted from the lips of

the hon. member far North Toronto (Mr. Foster) can mean only one thing, and that is that if the Conservatives were in power they would heighten the protection to agricultural implements and those other items I have indicated, and instead of having a lower duty we would have increased duties.
I have no desire to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but I would like to know if he supported the motion in 1907 to reduce the duties on agricultural implements?
If the Jion. member or any other member of his party were ever sufficiently brave to divide this House and place on record how the different men voted, I should be the most surprised man in Ottawa.

We had a division.
Mr.' KNOWLES. Can the hon. member find a ' Hansard ' showing the division? These h*n. gentlemen did not dare divide this House, and put themselves on record but they divided the committee where they knew they were safe, because in the Committee the votes of the different members is not recorded.
Did I not place myself on record? Did the hon. gentleman put himself on record?
I neither know nor care whether the hon. gentleman put himself on record.
I would like to have had an opportunity of voting for the motion which the hon. gentleman had on the paper last year, but which he never presented.

With regard to the policy of the Conservative party I just wish to read what the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) said with regard to the tariff. In 1903, he moved :
That this House, regarding the present tariff as unsatisfactory, is of opinion that this country requires a declared policy of such adequate protection to its labour, agricultural products, manufactures and industries as will at all times secure the Canadian market for Canadians.
I have been oareful to have these different utterances and declarations of the leaders of the Conservative party placed upon record, and there are no more important utterances than those made by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) and north Lanark (Mr. Thoburn), in which they declared that the tariff, instead of being lowered, should be increased, so in, answer to my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), I may say we have ample grounds for believing that if the Conservatives came into power they would increase protection.
Regarding the great questions brought before this government by the very large deputation from the West, I wish to say a word or two. I wish also to refer to the views expressed by one or two of the prominent members of the Liberal-Conservative party regarding the request by the agricultural deputation which came here and interviewed the government on the 16th December last. One of them, namely, the hon. member from North Toronto (Mr. Foster), in a letter to the ' Canadian Century ' of Montreal, writes of the request of the agriculturists that was placed before the government in this Chamber:
Their full realization would involve little short of revolution in principles and methods at present followed.
And further on, speaking of the chilled meat industry and the request in relation to it made by the farmers, he says:
This means that all the capital slfall be first provided and all the risks run by the state, and that all the profits shall accrue to the producers of food animals.
And he adds that these views,
-would, when fully embodied, socialize the entire economic system of the country.
And later on in the same letter-written by the hon. gentleman to the ' Canadian Century ' of January 14,-he says, speaking of the farmers' request in relation to elevators :
But here again the cost of elevators on both oceans and at many ports, and also on the lakes involves the pocket of every taxpayer in Canada. It is state aid that is invoked and state aid for the profit and advantage of a class.
And again, in the same article:
How would the tariff proposals of the deputation, so definitely expressed, so insistently demanded and pressed for immediate adoption, affect all this development?
He had been referred to the development of Canada generally.
Is it certain that their adoption would prove a panacea even for all the ills complained of as attaching to the farmers' vocation? Is it quite clear to the minds of the deputation what effect this sudden and pervasive change in our fiscal policy would have on all other interests and on the general development of our national ideal? These things .must be made very clear before the demands of even so intelligent and strong a deputation can hope for a favourable verdict from the grand jury of the nation. And when such proposals are transplanted from the atmosphere of the club or association, where but one interest is uppermost and one view favoured to the forum of the whole country the perspective changes, and other interests crowd to the foreground.
And, still later:

The out in duties is not to be exercised with discrimination, it is to be arbitrary and horizontal and instantaneous. No legislation was ever proposed on so inconsiderate and mechanical a basis.
It needs but a moment's reflection to visualize the resulting confusion, the crash of business enterprises, the depreciation and dislocation and loss of capital, the stoppage of industries, the non-employment of wage earners and the transfer of capital and labour to other countries.
I read those words to show that, much as hon. gentlemen opposite who come from the west may endeavour to have us believe that the true friend of the western agriculturist is the Conservative party, in my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) at least they find a man who will not support their views, differing, conscientiously no doubt, from them. It is well that the farmers of the west should know that whatever care and caution the Prime Minister may have exercised in not unduly and hastily committing himself to their view's, there is one of the foremost leaders of the Conservative party in the person of the hon. member from North Toronto (Mr. Foster), ready voluntarily to place himself on record as throwing cold water in the strongest way on the views of those who travelled so far to make their representations to this government.
My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) has dealt with the question of protection in such a way that I desire to take advantage of this opportunity to give my view's on this general subject. I do not know that, even on my own side, my views will be shared in altogether; I .very much question if they will. I think that protection is a system of extortion; I think it is class legislation. These things, of course, must strike a man very largely according to the viewpoint from which he sees them. I have tried, with any little thinking power I have, to look at this thing as carefully and fairly as I could. I do not wish, because I am a western man, to say things that I would not say if I were an eastern man; but I believe that, wdiether I be western or eastern, whether I w'ere interested and associated with those interested in manufacturing or with those interested in agriculture, my opinion would be the same-that protection is an artificial, arbitrary way of making a certain favoured class prosperous at the expense of another class. It is said that the farmers of the w'est are so prosperous that they should not mind this. I think that is beside the question. If a man is making all kinds of money, that does not justify me in taking from him a five-cent piece. I do not say that there are not other reasons which might be given in favour of protection, I but I do say that this argument that the * Mr. KNOWLES.
farmers are prosperous is, to my mind, idle, unnecessary, a waste of time; if protection be wrong on other grounds, it cannot be justified by such an argument as this.
That was the Prime Minister's answer to the delegation-that they had got rich in a few years and could stand it.

That was one of his observations; it is not his answer, and more than that, he did not say that they could stand it. His answer will be given in good time. He has been in his present position for fourteen years, and hon. gentlemen opposite have learned, to their sorrow, that he is able to solve problems presented to him. We are not afraid concerning his answer; and when that answer is given, I doubt not it will be as satisfactory to the people of the Dominion of Canada as the answers he has given to other pressing questions have been; and 1 believe he can go on giving equally satisfactory answers as long as he cares to retain his present office.
I believe that protection takes certain articles and by an artificial, and I believe a wrong, system, makes them a source of additional cost to the purchaser and additional profit to the seller. I do not think I need to stop to prove that the purchaser pays for protection. If any man thinks that protection does not raise prices, then what good does he find in protection? If any manufacturer says he does not get a higher price for his articles because they are protected, his mouth is closed when we propose to take his protection away. Protection can be of no good to any man unless it protects. Between ourselves and everything that we want there are obstacles. We want food, and clothes for example, and there are obstacles in the way of obtaining them and protection steps in and adds to these difficulties.

Will the hon. member (Mr. Knowles), allow me to ask him a question ? How is it that freetraders want to get into the United States in order to get cheap goods, when protective duties are so high in the United States ?
I do not understand the question.
I do not think you do. Why are the free traders so anxious to get into the United States to get cheap goods, where they have such high protection ?

Because we want cheap goods. My opinion is that it is only a foolish man who rejoices because goods are dear. I cannot see anything to be gained, if I have $10 to go to market, and I am charged higher prices

The hon. gentleman has not answered my question. If his argument is good and protection raises prices, why do people want to go into the United States, where protective duties are so high in order to get cheap goods ?

I make the statement that protection in Canada Taises the price of goods in Canada and protection in the United States raises the price of goods in the United States. I do not say that, if two countries are protected, they will necessarily have tne same cost prices, one protected country may be cheaper or dearer than another. But what are we protected against? The hon. member for Portage la Prairie, if I understood him Tightly, at the beginning of his address, seemed to say that free traders were inconsistent because they were against being protected against cheaper things. Suppose a man goes to buy a horse and the housewife goes to buy her house supplies, each having so much money, would they come home discouraged because they had got into a cheap market? Why should we regard a nation differently ? Should we say that it is going to be a profit to our nation if we, by artificial means, bring about a condition of things under which the things which we are to purchase are made expensive ?
The protection which we have to-day in Canada is not as heavy, not as vicious, I may say, as what they have in the United States; but it is one that is sufficient materially to increase the cost of the ordinary necessities which the people of this country, especially the agriculturists, have occasion to purchase. Let us take for example boots and shoes. My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie read certain statistics showing that there were so many million dollars worth of boots and shoes manufactured in Canada, and so many million dollars worth imported. I do not know what the proportion is. But let us suppose that to the consumer the increased cost of boots and slioes, for example, is a million dollars, because of protection. Now where does that million dollars go ? It all depends upon what proportion of those goods we use come from foreign countries and what proportion is produced in this country. Suppose we import ten per cent of those boots and shoes, if we import ten per cent it means that ten per cent of that additional cost of one million dollars will go into the public revenue, and that ninety per cent will go into the pockets of those who are manufacturing boots and shoes. Suppose we import just half and half, it will mean that fifty per cent will go into the revenue and fifty per cent will go to the private manufacturer. Suppose, on the other hand, we import ninety per cent and use only ten per cent of the home product, then, of course, ten
per cent will go into the pockets of the manufacturers, and ninety per cent into the coffers of the government. So either directly or indirectly, on every thing which We purchase which is inflated in value because of the tariff, we are making a gift to the manufacturer of that increased price which he gets by reason of the tariff. I believe that every -homesteader in my riding who, after his twelve months' toil with his horses and his oxen, comes into town to make his purchases after he has sold liis grain, if he has a certain number of dollars to his credit, because of his labour, he directly, as well as indirectly, makes the protected manufacturer of Canada, a gift of a certain percentage of his earnings, just as truly as if he bought a draft in the bank and sent it to Montreal or Toronto or Hamilton, or any other place where the protected manufacturer may be in business. I believe that the labourer, when the day is done and he goes home with his dollar or his two dollars in his pocket, and buys protected supplies, gives twenty-five, or thirty, or fifty cents of his day's earnings to the protected manufacturer, just as surely as if he sent it to him in an envelope. Even the poor washerwoman who has earned seventy-five cents a day and goes to the store to buy a woollen muffler for her child, even she has to pay her little tribute to these manufacturers out of her poverty. I believe that not only in this instance, but in every instance, which you may mention, and to which you may apply this principle, it is not only expensive to the individual but it is expensive to the nation as well. Protection in Canada has had the effect of raising up a few millionaires. How has i't made them ? It has made them by giving them inflated values for their products.
Would the hon. gentleman tell me how he would raise the $150,000,000 that we now have to expend, if he wiped out protection ?
I think under a ten per cent tariff we would raise far more revenue than we do now.
Then this poor woman who works for seventy-five cents a day and has to pay a portion of that to the manufacturer, would, under the hon. gentleman's theory, have to pay a direct tax.
In any case, she would have to pay much less than she does now, and you could not make the poor washerwoman pay anything to the manufacturer.
The question is how you will raise a revenue if you wipe out protection?

A lower tariff will bring in more revenue. We now have a lower

tariff than our friends had when they were in power, and twice as much revenue.

Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to tell us why, when the present government increased the duty on leather, and when he was trying to make us believe a while ago that the government were reducing the duty on most articles, why did he allow that to be done without opposing the government?

The hon. gentleman had better put that question on the Order Paper. If the citizens of the United States had to pay a direct tax to Carnegie, or Morgan, or Schwab, or any other of those millionaires there would be a revolution. Yet I say that would be no more unjust than to make a man pay an artificial price on the goods that any of those millionaires manufacture.

The farmer is a manufacturer of pork, of butter, of cheese. Does the ten cents a pound, or the four cents a pound duty on those articles have the effect of increasing their price to the washerwoman and the labouring man?

If they had to import them, it would. At the same time there is no question in my mind that the price of butter and other agricultural products is set by the price in Liverpool. The hon. gentleman as a manufacturer may think he knows better about those things than I do. But I understand that the price of almost all farm products is set by the foreign market. I say this imposition which is placed upon the people by an indirect tax is in principle just as wrong as if it were a direct tax placed upon them for the purpose of creating manufacturing barons by paying them a certain tribute. In my opinion it makes a privileged class, a class that has no inherent or vested right to have this privilege continued for ever. A few days ago our friends the manufacturers presented this government with a memorial setting forth their views and they asked that nothing should be done to jeopardize their interests. I noticed that the sole thought which seemed to run through their memorial and all their representations, was that they had a vested right, and were entitled to demand that they should be looked after by this government, that at the expense of the consumer they were for ever to be hedged about by a wall of protection so that no person could ever come near to them or their belongings, but that they were for ever to be kept in affluence. Mr. S-'caker. T say that I am opposed to any such theory. I believe that the manufacturers of this country have no vested right to D>p m-roetuation of the privileges they now eojov Tt may be that as a matter of Mr. KNOWLES.
decency they should not be cut off too suddenly; but because a man has been enjoying a favour from the government year after year, or even for generation after generation, is that a valid reason why it should never be taken from him? If he is allowed to continue in its enjoyment, it will be by the grace of the government, by the generosity of the people of Canada. As I said in the few words I quoted from a speech of mine some years ago, we might just as well make them a gift, just as well make them a bonus, just as well put our hands in our pockets and help them that way, as by the indirect method of a protective tariff. In this memorial which I hold in my hand there are one or two things I will refer to. One of their chief arguments seems to be that they say they have created a home market for the farmer. I had always thought that we were an agricultural country. I had always thought that the nrotectionist tariff which has been in existence for thirty years had created the manufacturers. I had thought that it was the consumers of the country who, by their generosity, their patriotism and national spirit, had made it possible for the manufacturers to come into existence. But, they seemed to think that they have made a market for us as if we had come here and found them. Not a word of gratitude from them, not the slightest appreciation of the fact that Canada for thirty years has held them up by protection, not a word of that but rather they come here boasting of the fact that they have made home markets for us. What are the home markets that we have? They are good for the fruit and vegetable men, I suppose, but those are comparatively few in number. In so far as the great agricultural business of this country goes the home market which the manufacturers have made in Canada is, in my opinion, a very insignificant quantity.
Is the hon. gentleman not aware that there is a large deputation of farmers here now asking the Prime Minister to give them protection?

I do not think I deserve to be interrupted quite as often as I have been. I do not interrupt hon. gentlemen. I can only flatter mvself that perhaps I touch their protectionist feelings a little. The market which the manufacturers have spoken about and boasted so much of, is, in my opinion, a pretty good joke as one of the sneakers said when the farmers interviewed the Prime Minister on the 16th December. Our great nroductions on the farm are the products of the field, of the dairy, of the orchard, ind the vast proportion of these things Inds its purchase price set by the foreign market. I believe that some of our northwest wheat is used in Ontario, but what

farmer in Saskatchewan or Alberta gets a five cent piece more for his year's crop because some wheat goes into mills in Ontario and Quebec? I believe that some of our wool is used in eastern Canada, but we have no protection on wool. There is no hedging about of the products of the farmer in that matter. The woollen men get the great bulk of their wool from the old country, and after all is said and done that is where the price of wool is set. So, with regard to butter and cheese; the price of the millions of dollars worth produced by the farmers of Canada is not set by the markets of Toronto, Hamilton, or London, but by the market price of Liverpool. Another feature of the memorial is where the manufacturers say that if there are going to be better trade relations with the United States we might as well stop building the Transcontinental railway, the Hudson Bay railway, and the Georgian Bay canal. I never heard of anything so ridiculous. We will still have our wheat in the west even if there should be one or two little manufacturing places in Ontario less prosperous with a lower tariff. It is an enormous piece of conceit, in my humble opinion, for the manufacturers to say that unless they get their way -we might as well stop building the National Transcontinental railway. The National Transcontinental railway will be built, there will be work for it to do and as I shall hope to show in a few minutes, there would be just as great prosperity or even greater prosperity if we were to do away more fully with this economic principle of protection.
The memorialists put forward one or two reasons why they advocate protection. One of the great reasons they give in favour of protection is that with the home market which they claim to have provided and which I say is a joke, they give employment to men. In the first place I am not sure but that they would give even greater employment to men if we had a lower tariff, because living would be cheaper, the necessities of life would be more easily obtained and men could live for less money than they now possibly can. As has been pointed out, one of the great manufacturing concerns of this country, the Massey-Harris Company, has been so unduly prosperous	under protection
that it has $3,000,000 with which to go over into the United States and acquire another plant.	If protection were
ever to be justifiable it is justifiable only as a great necessity. It is class legislation, it is privilege and it should be justified only as a very great necessity, or as something which is indispensable. But, when we find that by reason of this policy of protection under which the farmers and the people have to pay enhanced prices to enable the manufacturers to carry on business without
going to smash, and when these manufacturers are able to present halls to the city of Toronto, and are possessed of $3,000,000 with which to go into the United States and purchase a business there it will be seen that they are not as near a smash as they thought they were and that they have prospered exceedingly at the hands of the government and the people. There is one manufacturer who said that the tariff should be raised as high as Haman's gallows. I have nothing to do with that man's personal business, but I am informed that even without a tariff as high as Haman's gallows he has gathered to himself no small fortune. Even if the worst came to the worst, labour is only a means to an end. The highest ideal of men is not to gather themselves together under an economic system by which there will be labour provided. If labour is the onl-y thing why not make the people labour more, why not break our machines so that men will have to do more hard work? But, it is not labour that you want. Why not do any one of a hundred ridiculous things so as to increase the labour of the country? That is not what we are protected for. The manufacturers practically say to us:	Give us your contribution, protect us, give us these inflated prices so that we can hire you, your brothers and sisters and your children yet unborn. They are going to give labour to. us if only we will protect them enough. I do not know that that is any great advantage to hold out to us. The manufacturers say that they are going to make a labour market for us if we will give them protection, but we do not take very much stock in that. We do not want to lie down before them. We do not want our brothers and our sisters to be their coachmen and footmen and servants. We are to give them the opportunity to amass riches and they are to have us and our children at their service. To that we say that we will get along very well for burselves and we say that the manufacturers who have been unduly protected might better look out and try to make an honest living for themselves while we will look out for ourselves.
I understand that there are fifteen cabinet ministers in this House. Suppose, for example, that they were off in a colony living by themselves. We will suppose that one of them-the Minister of Customs-says to the other fourteen: Now, if you will just give me 10 per cent additional on everything I produce in this colony of ours I will do wonderful things for you; we will all live on the same footing, except that I will have an increased price of 10 per cent for what I produce; I will have a fine home, a few clubs, automobiles, silk hats, and in return I will furnish employment for yourselves and your children-they shall be employed, some in buttoning up.

my daughters' dresses, some in shining my sons' shoes, and all you have to do to secure this employment is to give this extra 10 per cent to me. I fancy that the other fourteen cabinet ministers would say to the Minister of Customs: That is very fine for you, but it is too thin, and they would be right in doing so. If that went on for a year the Minister of Customs would naturally be amassing great possessions and his brother ministers would be likely to say to him: This is a privilege you cannot keep, and he would be fortunate if they did not take his ill-gotten gains away from him. So I say with regard to protection; I believe that the people of Canada will become alive to the injustice of this protection theory, and that the day will come when they will tell the manufacturers to endeavour to make their own way in the world without this tribute. The manufacturers sometimes say: What will become of us? Well, there is a fine country here; there is no trouble for anybody to make a living; the manufacturers and their families have a chance the same as anybody else. I have seen the manufacturers out west get after the farmers many and many a time when they get behind in their lien notes, and I never saw a manufacturer care so much what became of the homesteader; they employ the sheriff over and above what his legal exemptions were, there was very little mercy shown the farmer. If he asked:	What is going to
become of me, the answer usually was: We get our orders from London, or Hamilton, or from some other centre, and outside the protection afforded him by law they would skin him as close as they could skin him. The manufacturers now say: What is to become of us, our vested rights, and our millions that we have got by favours from the government?
It may be that the manufacturer should be decently dealt with, but he has no right or justice to demand from us a continuance of protection for one hour longer. I believe that as a nation we should produce these things which it is natural for us to produce, and what it is not natural for us to produce we should buy from the proceeds we obtain from those things which we can profitably produce. I think we should do as they do in England. If a manufacturer cannot make things go there he does not come to the government begging for protection and for a contribution; he endeavours to reorganize his system; he uses his brains; he endeavours to get more capital if it is needed; he endeavours to find new markets; he faces the world and does his business like an Englishman, or he fails in the attempt. Sir, I think our manufacturers should be willing, especially after all these years of protection they have Mr. KNOWLES.
had, to go out and face the world without this garment of protection round about them; I think they should battle for themselves and make a living in this world without an artificial contribution from the other people of Canada. It is nice to have manufacturers; it would be nice to grow oranges if we could, and I suppose if we went to enormous expense we could do so. But Providence has so created this part of North America that we are able profitably to grow certain things and to produce certain things, and certain things it may not be profitable for us to produce. If, for example, I have a field that will grow oats very well, but will not grow clover, and my neighbour has a field that will grow clover luxuriantly, but will scarcely grow oats at all, would I not be foolish if I kept scratching away at my ground in a vain attempt to grow clover, and would my neighbour not be foolish if he attempted to raise not only his own clover but his own oats? Would it not be wise for me to grow oats and for the other man to grow clover, and trade my oats for his clover?
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that every industry that must be protected and asks for protection, thereby makes a confession of pauperism ; thereby makes a confession of drawing the workman from more profitable departments of labour and placing him at something that is les3 profitable. The very fact that protection is asked by so many of our manufacturers is in itself a confession that they have put some of the labourers of our country to toil at something unprofitable, and where they must be supported by other labour which comes to the rescue by paying these enhanced prices. And as a principle of true economies I submit that no country should ever continue bolstering up and making contributions to any one favoured set of citizens. I submit that the true economic principle is that when a country cannot profitably produce a certain article she should produce what she can produce, and exchange it for that which the other country can produce profitably. There are certain things that every member of this House can produce. He may by his activity, whether professional or otherwise, produce something in this world, but there is probably not any one of us who could produce his own hat or his own suit of clothes, and so we go to our neighbour who can produce them. He would be exceedingly foolish who would insist on providing himself with his own clothes when the man who is engaged in that industry can produce them cheaper and better. So, the nation that artificially, arbitrarily, unnaturally, and unprofitably persists in producing something which it has to produce at an acknowledged loss, is a nation which does not follow the true and the best principles of economic government. A group of

men gather, we will say in Toronto, and they will have a talk there, and they will say that is a fine and nohle thing that tlie man in Halifax should trade with the man in Vancouver, 4,000 miles away, but it is an unpatriotic, and almost criminal thing that the man in St. John should trade with the man in Boston; they will say that the man in Charlottetown should trade with the man in Victoria, but the man in Toronto must not trade with the man in Buffalo, and the man in Winnipeg must not trade with the man in St. Paul. Did you ever hear, Mr. Speaker, of anything so artificial, so arbitrary. If it were not that we were used to it by long years of bolstering up such a theory, I do not believe we would put up with it whatever. On the very face of it the thing is absolutely wrong. Why cannot we trade with the people of France if we wish? Why, if I wish to, can I not buy from the people of the United States? Protection ! protection against whom? It is protection against ourselves that we are guilty of. We treat ourselves like little children, we cannot allow ourselves to do what we wish, and we gather in this parliament and we make a law binding ourselves and the people we represent not to do what we want to do. Well, Sir, I believe it is an unrighteous law. The experience is that scarcely one person out of ten is so conscientiously moral that he will ever bother himself about bringing things into the country without paying duty. We call it smuggling, but in a great many cases there is no sense of wrong in the man who is guilty of smuggling. Is not that a strong reason to bring us to believe that the thing which brings about such a condition is not right? I believe, Sir, that before many more generations have come the people of this world will rise to a knowdedge of the fact that protection is not only not right, but that it is not profitable. Did it ever strike you as being strange that the people of the United States should protect themselves against labour from here, and that -we should pro-' ect ourselves because we are afraid of the labourers of the United States? The people in Germany protect themselves against the people of France. Alsace and Lorraine used to be in France -and they had to be protected against Germany ; now they belong to Germany, -and they have to be protected against France. And so it is, the people of every country, except Great Britain, feel that they have to protect themselves against every other country, all afraid of one another and just like a lot of children they make these artificial rules binding themselves and tieing themselves up. I believe this fallacy obtains through the influence of the manufacturing barons who lead the people round and get them to. swallow these sophistries that
never should be put before the people. It may be said that it is more or less to the advantage of a nation to have its own home markets, and that indeed may be the ideal state. But are we anxious to have our own home markets? I should like to know how much this government spend a year sending men to Australia, to Holland, to Hong Kong, to Pekin, to all the countries of the earth trying to get markets that we can sell our goods in ; and yet we are paying an unearthly price to keep our products in our own market. We are paying large amounts to men to find places to which we can send our goods, and yet we are told by these hon. gentlemen that we must try to keep our goods in our home market. If the home market is the one where our goods find the most ready welcome and are most desired, there they should stay and not otherwise.
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), in speaking of infant industries, cited as his authority no less a person than the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), that at the inception of tariff duties there should naturally be a higher rate than after they had had time to get on their feet. Our infant industries were brought into their being in 1878, over 30 years ago. I am just old enough to be able to remember hearing them talk about infant industries in the early 80's. The early 90's came, we turned the cycle of the century, we are in another decade now, and we still have the infant industries. The great majority of those who created this policy, the great old fathers of Canada, have gone. A generation has come that had nothing at all to do with this policy when it was inaugurated-the infant industries are still there, still nursing, still sucking as it were, trying to get their food so easily, still the infant at the breast of the nation. They desire to be kept in this artificial and unnatural way. When is the day to come when they will not be infants ? I am asking that seriously, I represent I suppose about 60,000 people in the district of Moose-jaw, and I want to ask on behalf of my constituents when the time will come when manufacturers will stand on their feet like men and go out and face the trade competition of the United States and the rest of the world. Are they going to be infant industries forever ? They are grown, they are rich; one of them, can go to the United States and pay $3,000,000 to purchase another plant, and still the infant is fed up and fed up and fattened and fattened and it now has an idea that it always has -to be an infant and that it has some" vested right that never shall be taken from it.
