The hon. gentleman will, I am sure, pardon me if I do not refer at any particular length to the very interesting and voluminous speech he has given us. If I do not do so it is because he has simply delivered a disquisition upon general principles, upon the question of free trade versus protection, and has most carefully kept away from the question now before us. I looked for something more practical from him on this matter, and should have been pleased to hear from him whether he was prepared to support the motion of my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), or whether he was not. But he failed to give us the slightest indication on this point. He denounced the system of protection as an abominable one, as a system of extortion, as class legislation, but he should bear in mind that the hon. the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding), speaking for the government, admitted, only a short time ago, that the principle of protection was still embalmed in their policy. Therefore, in denouncing protection, the hon. gentleman is denouncing the very men whom he supports by his votes all the time. He may

raise Ms voice in favour of free trade, but actions speak louder than words, and when it comes to action we find him always with the party which has now adopted the principle of protection. Not only, as my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) pointed out, are the party opposite still a party of protection, but they have largely increased the protection on certain articles over what it was in 1896, when the Conservatives were in office. One special article was referred to to-day by my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie, and he offered the most abundant proof that the protection on that article had been increased by the present government, as it has been, I venture to say, on nearly every other article on which duty is levied.
Hear, hear.

This is rightly understood by this House and is partially accounted for by the large increase in prices which has taken place. The hon. gentleman devoted some time to the Manufacturers' Association, which he condemned in no measur'ed terms, as well as the deputation it sent the other day to the Prime Minister. But did that deputation ask for an increase in the duties? No, simply that the duties should not be interfered with. The manufacturers are satisfied with the duties as they are at present. How comes it then that the hon. gentleman can be supporting the government? I am afraid he has taken a leaf out of the book of the Prime Minister, who, while practising protection still gets up and proclaims himself a free trader. He reminds me of the men who will go to temperance meetings and advocate total abstinence but who have no scruples in taking liquor themselves. The Prime Minister says he is a free trader; and yet, for fifteen years, he has steadily and consistently practised protection. Now, I would like to have asked the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) had he not so quickly left the chamber at the close of his speech, how it was that hd did not preach this gospel of free trade last year. At the beginning of last session' he placed on the Order Paper the following notice:-
Mr. Knowles.-Proposed Resolution.-That in the opinion of this House it is desirable that the government should at an early date take into serious consideration the reduction of the tariff duties of Canada, especially with respect to such articles and commodities as are the necessaries of the agricultural classes.
That resolution remained at the head of the Order Paper practically throughout the whole of the session. Almost every day when notices of motions were called, the hon. gentleman had the privilege, if he chose to exercise it, of moving that resolution. And yet, from the beginning Mr. LAKE.
of the session to the end of it, he remained in his seat and declined to advocate in this House those principles over wdiich he has been so eloquent to-day. It seems to me that he was deterred from doing so not only by his own feelings towards the gov-i ernment but by the pressure which was brought to bear upon him by hon. members on the other side who, while they' cry ' Free trade ' as their policy so persistently practise protection. But after all, this proposed resolution of the hon. member for Moosejaw was a very mild one for a man who speaks of himself as such a confirmed free trader. It was a resolution which everybody in this House could have voted for. We could all agree that these matters should be ' taken into serious consideration ' by the government. The government would have taken them into serious consideration, and again we would have followed in the same old way and the same old policy would have been carried out. Here the hon. member for Moosejaw has an opportunity to vote for and advocate a resolution which is along the lines of his proposed resolution of last year, the difference being that this, is specific and deals with the article which the farmers most of all use, the article which they only of all people in the country have to use. And yet, even though he has made a speech of an hour and a quainter or more he has not advocated that resolution by so much as a single wrord. I do not intend to speak at any length upon this question, chiefly because the-hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) has argued the point with such extraordinary ability and complete-* ness that the case, when he left it, to my mind, was absolutely unanswerable-and probably that is the reason why the hon. member for Moosejaw saw fit to talk altogether aside from the question in an endeavour to lead the House away from the point at issue.
For my part, I have many a time expressed, both in this House _ and out of it, my opinions on this question ; and I have more than expressed my opinions, I have backed up my opinions by my vote. The hon. member for Moosejaw cannot say so much, for, though he had the opportunity of voting for the reduction of the duty on agricultural implements, he spoke against it and voted against it or refrained from voting altogether. The farmers, also, very recently laid their views in regard to the question of free trade and protection before this House. They have done it with singular ability. And I think the hon. member for Moosejaw might have left it at that ; the views of the farmers have been laid before the House better and more clearly certainly than he has been able to lay his views before the House, and I think the members

of the House do not take as much interest in the views of the hon. member as they do in the views of the large delegation that waited upon the government last month. To my mind, the main principle we ought to have in view in dealing with such questions as this is laid down in the tariff policy declared toy the leader of the opposition in what is now known as the Halifax platform :
A policy which will promote the production within Canada of all useful articles and commodities that can be advantageously produced or manufactured from or by means of our natural resources, having due regard to the interests of the consumer as well as to the just claims of our wage-earning community.
We have a great country, a country unsurpassed in vast natural resources, and it should be the aim of the legislation of this parliament to promote the development of these resources. And I believe that our agricultural resources are the greatest of all ; in no other part of the world, I believe, can their inexhaustible wealth be surpassed. Whatever we do to assist the agriculturist not only adds to the material wealth of the country, but it also assists all other branches of industry by cheapening the cost of food to the labourer and the artisan. Under modern conditions, in order to carry out successful husbandry, it is absolutely essential that the farmer should provide himself with expensive agricultural implements. I look upon these implements as being exactly in the same category as the raw material of the manufacturers. The farmer is unable to profitably produce from his farm unless he provides himself with modern agricultural machinery. If you assist the manufacturer, as you are doing, in cheapening his raw material, I consider it to be your bounden duty to give as much assistance-or, indeed, a great deal more assistance-to the agriculturist who is developing the most important of our great natural resources. Especially do I think you should grant him a policy which will cheapen his agricultural machinery, because I believe you could do so without any loss to the existing industries of this country, and without the loss of a day's labour to a single artisan employed in those industries. I do not intend to indulge in violent language in regard to onr manufacturers, because I do not feel any particular violence towards them. I leave it to the Prime Minister and his Cabinet to use such expressions as that ' manufacturers are robbers ' or ' the system of protection is a system of slavery,'-I gladly leave such expressions to these hon. gentlemen who used them years ago. I would like to suggest to them that if their statements at that time were true, that the manufacturers were robbers, then they are
now in the position of being the abettors of robbers. If protection was slavery then, these hon. gentlemen are in the position of slave drivers. But as I said, I will leave such expressions entirely to those who use them, and I will not indulge in any such language.
The National Policy, as I understand it, was intended to protect our infant industries until they could stand alone, to protect them from undue and unfair competition from outside. Now, the Minister of Customs, differing from the Minister of Finance in this respect, has told us that the sole principle which the government should apply in dealing with the tariff is the principle of tariff for revenue only. Then he stated in this House that even if the Mas-sey-Harris Company and other implement firms were becoming very wealthy, that was no reason for reducing the amount of tariff protection they enjoy. He argued that it would be unfair to give one manufacturer only twenty per cent, while others had thirty or thirty-five per cent. That is the argument, apparently, of gentlemen who advocate a tariff for revenue only, just as if it was a matter of giving favours which were at the disposal of the government, according to one manufacturer thirty-five per cent protection in order to increase his profits, and to another only twenty per cent. To my mind this is an entirely wrong principle. But even if it were right, it would defeat -its own ends. A tariff which prevents imports altogether will raise no revenue at all, and it seems to me that is the point which is being appproached in respect of the tariff on agricultural implements. As set forth by my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie a reduction of the tariff will sometimes produce an increased revenue, and I am confident that in this particular case a reduction would produce a corresponding increase in the revenue.
Personally I believe that the agricultural implement industry is unduly protected. I regret that I have no definite information upon which to base that opinion, but we are all able to judge from outside indications. Some four or five years ago the government appointed a tariff commission to go through the country and take evidence to ascertain whether the tariff should be increased or lowered, or whether any change should he made in it. That commission was composed of three able gentlemen, and so far as I can see, the course they pursued was to bring witnesses before them, cross-examine them as to their views, then argue the point with them, and by their superior ability in debate, to prove to the unfortunate witness thaA he must be wrong in his opinions. To my mind such a course as that was simply throwing away the large amount of money expended on the commission. In order to enable this

House to come to an intelligent conclusion as to whether any industry was sufficiently protected, the commission should have inquired into the cost of manufacturing. They should have gone, for instance, to the agricultural implement manufacturers and found out from them, on oath, what the cost was of manufacturing various kinds of implements, then the commission would have been able to judge whether twenty per cent wa.s an adequate protection or whether it was more than sufficient My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie proved that nearly twenty-two per cent is to-day enjoyed by the manufacturers of binders.
Now, the Minister of Customs was asked, when the tariff was being debated in this House, why the commission did not inquire into the cost of manufacturing agricultural implements, and he gave this answer: We did inquire as to the cost of producing machines, but they would not give us the absolute cost. It would be a pathetic sight, Mr. Speaker, _ to see that venerable gentleman pleading with the manufacturers to tell the commission what it cost to manufacture these agricultural implements, while the haughty manufacturer was standing up and positively refusing to give the information. To my mind that is the only information which would be of use to this 'House in dealing with this question. Failing such positive information as to whether they are actually making an undue profit, we have to judge by outside indications. We have to judge by the fact that the implement manufacturers of this country have a world-wide trade; that one of these companies boasts of being the greatest company manufacturing agricultural implements under the British flag; that in all other countries they are able to compete with all other manufacturers, including those of the United States; that a farmer can obtain a cheaper binder in some other countries, in Great Britain for instance, than in the Northwest. We have further the evidence laid before this House this afternoon by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, evidence given before the United States Congress by men who have been manufacturing in both countries, that the cost was about the same in both countries. Another fact which seems to show that the manufacturers of agricultural implements are being unduly protected at the present time, is that they are going into business in the United States. Let me for a moment refer to some ancient history, let me refer to a speech made by the Minister of Agriculture at Moosomin, on the 4th of October, 1894, and which I find quoted by Mr. Davin in the ' Hansard ' of 1899, page 5863. Mr. Fisher said:
As a farmer he was not satisfied with the reduction which had been made in the agri-Mr. LAKE.
cultural implement duties, because the United states Congress had made a standing offer of reciprocity in implements, and it was the duty of the Canadian government to take advantage of that.
Later on he said:
Referring to the Massey-Harris combine, he claimed that the fact that these people spoke of going to the United States to fight the Yankees in their own markets, showed that the Canadian manufacturers were able to get along without protection. Canadians were able to hold their own with the Yankees in any walk of life. The Massey-Harris Company got protection; why should not the farmers?
Now, Mr. Speaker, if the conditions upon which that argument was based were true then, how much more true are they at the present day, under the enormous increase, in the agricultural implement industry, which has taken place? That which was foreshadowed by the Minister of Agriculture has come to pass, and the Massy-Harris Company, according to press reports of interviews given by the head of that company, have purchased the Johnson Harvester Company of Batavia, in the State of New York. They are putting into that business a sum of between two and three million dollars. The Johnson Company is one of the oldest and best known companies in the United States, employing at the present time 1,200 men, which number the Massy-Harris Company propose to increase to 1,500 or 2,000. The sum which is being given for the interest which the Massey-Harris people are getting in that industry has been made out of the people of this country, chiefly under the protection which has been afforded them by the government which is at present in power. The chief reason which was given by the head of the Massey-Harris Company for going into the United States were the difficulty of obtaining an extension of ground area, and he also said that goods can be manufactured for less in the United States, thereby showing himself at variance with the sworn testimony given before the committee of the United States Congress only a short time ago. Mr. Jones was asked whether they had been influenced by the reciprocity talk and he refused to give an answer in regard to that question, leaving it to be supposed that he did not wish for reciprocity and that he would like the people to believe that they had been influenced to some extent by the reciprocity talk. Are we now to have the reciprocity in agricultural implements with the United States which was advocated by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), with his chief sitting beside him on the platform in Moosomin in 1894 ? Were the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture serious and in earnest when they made their statements

at Moosomin ? Have they done anything to put .their preaching into practice ? They have not, and the people of this country well know how to take any promises that they may make to them in the future ? I have already referred to the results of the policy of the government with regard to the duty of, agricultural implements. For many years they have increased the protection on these implements by the simple expedient, as was pointed out this afternoon of increasing the valuation upon them. The consequence is that higher duties have been paid and are being paid at the present moment according to the best of my information on every class of implement imported into this country than when the Conservatives were in power, previous to 1896. There are other ways in which .they have brought this about, such as the small expedients'5 of the present government contained in its customs regulations and the dumping clause. The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), candidly admitted to the House, at the time of the tariff revision in 1907, that they proposed, when nominally reducing the duty on threshing machines, to offset that by increasing the valuation under which threshing machines might be brought into this country. He said: We have reduced the duty from 25 to 20 per cent, but we have put the valuation higher, so that practically we shall collect about the same duty as we did before.
I do not wish to see any legitimate industry of this country killed by unfair competition from outside. It is my desire that all the industries in the country should prosper and that there may be abundant work for the artisan and farm labourer. But, I do not wish to see any industry make exorbitant profits at the expense of the people. I believe that in certain instances that is being done, under the high protective policy of the present administration. The particular instance which was brought to your attention this afternoon, that of agricultural implements, was abundantly proved by the hon. member who brought it forward. He also showed to what an enormous extent the capitalization of these agricultural implement industries had increased of recent years,-money which has been made out of the consumers of this country, money which has been practically exacted from the farming community, money which, if it had been left with the farming community, would have enormously increased the area of productiveness, which would have very materially added to the wealth of the whole country and which, I believe, would have reduced the cost of food to the consumers in the manufacturing centres. I believe that in all industries there should be a reasonable profit for the capital invested and for the risks that confront people who invest their
money in manufacturing, but I believe that the government should keep the closest supervision, by means of a permanent commission or otherwise, over the cost of manufacturing and over the prices which are being charged for the goods which are manufactured by these concerns and that when more than a legitimate profit is being exacted from the consumer the government should step in and take away the duty. That is the policy which is in force in the Antipodes. If I recollect aright, within the last two or three years, the government of Australia have placed a law upon their statute-books which enables them to take away altogether the duty which is imposed upon the importation of certain agricultural implements if the manufacturers in the country charge too high a price for those implements. I believe that our climate, our natural resources and the wonderful virility of our people are destined to make us a great manufacturing nation. I believe that we shall be able to compete in the markets of the whole world and in certain industries, I believe we can compete in the markets of the whole world at the present moment. I believe that in certain industries we can compete with protection very much lower than that which is contained m the present tariff. I do not think it was ever the intention of the government of Sir John Macdonald or his successors that, when industries were able to manufacture at a reasonable profit to themselves and to compete with the products of the United States and other foreign nations, they should receive any more protection. I believe that at that time it was the intention that as industries grew to manhood their protection should be reduced until the duty merely maintained tariff for the reason of revenue to carry on the government of the country. Our agricultural implement manufacturers were novices when they commenced and they were protected, but they have grown to be veterans now, and the time has come when their protection should be very materially reduced or taken off altogether. I beg to declare myself completely in favour of the resolution which has been moved by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen).

Mr. Speaker, as this a question that is of great interest to the people in my riding, I cannot cast a silent vote upon it. The resolution of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) is in line with current ideas m the province of Alberta, and I heartily concur in his conclusions.
1 speak for the Conservative members from the province of Alberta on this side of the House. Any one who knows the history of the National Policy agitation knows that that struggle

was for a national tariff policy. Let me read the National Policy resolutions of March 7, 1878, which was the basis of the national policy that was subsequently inaugurated by Sir John, and has dominated "tire fiscal policy of this country ever since :
'That the Speaker do not now leave the Chair, but that this House is of the opinion that the welfare of Canada requires the adoption of a national policy which, by a judicious readjustment of the tariff, will benefit and foster the agricultural, the mining, the manufacturing and other interests of the Dominion; that such a policy will retain in Canada thousands of our fellow countrymen now obliged to expatriate themselves in search of the employment denied them at home, will restore prosperity to our struggling industries, now so sadly depressed, will prevent Canada from being made a sacrifice market, will encourage and. develop an active interprovincial trade, and moving, as it ought to do, in the direction of a reciprocity of tariffs with our neighbours, so far as the varied interests of Canada may demand, will greatly tend to procure for this country, eventually, a reciprocity of trade/
Now, Sir, you will note that the interests of agriculture are given first place in that resolution. Alexander Hamilton, who was the first great advocate of a national tariff system in the United States placed the interests of agriculture first, and _we find in every country that has a national tariff that-' the interests of the predominant industry are given first place. The greatest industry in this country is agriculture, and whilst the farmers have always shown themselves ready and willing to carry' their end of the log, they should not be asked to bear the whole burden. The tariff on agricultural implements is too high, that is to say especially on some lines, and the interests of the farmers should not -be sacrificed for the interests of the implement trusts.	_
I have quoted the National Policy resolution, moved by Sir John Macdonald to show that this policy placed the interest of the farmers first. The Liberal press is fond of linking the -Conservative party up to high protections, and it is time this lie was nailed. Liberal speakers and Liberal associations throughout this country have during the last 12 or 15 years endeavoured to convince the farmers of Canada that they were the low tariff party, and even the hon. gentleman from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) has to-day advocated free trade. But, it has been shown by the hon. mem-

ber for Portage la Prairie (Mr. - Meighen) that to-day the farmers are paying a higher duty on the implements he mentioned than they were paying under the Conservative government. The larmers of Canada are better posted now than they were years ago and they understand these things. It does not make much difference to them whether a party calls itself free trade or protectionist if they have to pay $23 -duty on a binder when they only paid from $16 to $18 under the Conservative government which was called protectionist. That little game is played out -amongst the farmers of Canada, and they have come to realize that they have been bamboozled -by this government for the last 10 or 12 years. The Conservative policy has always been a national policy which placed the interests of the farmers first ; I am a believer in that principle. Sir John Macdonald, on many occasions emphasized the fact that when an industry had -bv _ a national tariff policy been established in this country, and had grown sufficiently strong to walk alone, and had taken its competitive share of foreign trade, a tariff on that line of product was no longer necessary. No one will deny that the manufacturers of binders and mowers have reached that position, as our annual statistical tables show us that they are large exporters of these articles. There may, however, be other articles in the classification of other agricultural implements which are not put in that position, but on these lines at least the tariff is not necessary. I will go even further than the mover of this resolution (Mr. Meighen) and would say that the time has arrived when the duty should be taken entirely off -binders and mowers, and such articles as the great implement trusts of this country find they can ship out of Canada and sell in foreign countries against foreign competition.
If the west is to succeed and it is succeeding, if Canada is going to be a great country no man nor no party can afford to ignore'the greatest industry in the country, namely agriculture. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, while I would like to go even further than the -hon. member for Portage la Prairie and have the duty removed, I give my enthusiastic support to this resolution as a step in the right direction, believing that in doing so, I am consistent as a believer in the National Policy, and as a Conservative.
At six o'clock, the House adjourned.
